front: {{c1::Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase}} is the committed, rate-limiting PPP step; it is inhibited by its product {{c2::NADPH}} and induced by {{c3::insulin}}.

front: {{c1::GLUT2}} (liver, beta cells) is high-$K_m$ and insulin-independent; {{c2::GLUT4}} (muscle, adipose) is insulin-recruited.

front: 1,3-BPG's high-energy {{c1::acyl phosphate}} lets {{c2::phosphoglycerate kinase}} form ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
why: Substrate-level phosphorylation at PGK is an outline-level glycolysis concept

front: A cell needs ribose 5-phosphate but no NADPH (rapid division, ample reducing power). How does the PPP accommodate this?
why: PPP flexibility for ribose vs NADPH; passage-level second step

front: Classic galactosemia = {{c1::GALT}} deficiency; {{c2::galactokinase}} deficiency causes mainly cataracts via {{c3::galactitol}}.

front: Contrast glycogenesis and glycogenolysis and their hormonal control.
why: Glycogenesis vs glycogenolysis and their hormonal control is core fed/fasting content

front: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase is allosterically inhibited by {{c1::AMP}} and {{c2::fructose 2,6-bisphosphate}}.

front: Fructose: {{c1::fructokinase}} makes F1P, {{c2::aldolase B}} cleaves it, and the carbons enter glycolysis below {{c3::PFK-1}}.

front: G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis because red cells cannot regenerate {{c1::NADPH}} to keep {{c2::glutathione}} reduced.

front: Glucagon acts via {{c1::PKA}} phosphorylation of the bifunctional enzyme, activating hepatic {{c2::FBPase-2}} and lowering {{c3::fructose 2,6-bisphosphate}}.

front: Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves by {{c1::phosphorolysis}} using $P_i$ to release {{c2::glucose 1-phosphate}}, with {{c3::pyridoxal phosphate}} as cofactor.

front: Glycogen synthase cannot start a chain de novo. What primes glycogen synthesis?

front: Glycogen synthase is inactivated by phosphorylation via {{c1::GSK-3 and PKA}}, and reactivated when insulin stimulates {{c2::protein phosphatase 1 (PP1)}}.

front: Hemoglobin A1c reflects roughly {{c1::3 months}} of glycemia because it forms {{c2::nonenzymatically}} and red cells survive about 120 days.

front: Hepatic {{c1::glucokinase}} has a {{c2::high}} $K_m$ (~10 mM) and, unlike hexokinase, is NOT inhibited by {{c3::glucose 6-phosphate}}.
why: Glucokinase vs hexokinase Km and G6P inhibition is a high-frequency distinction

front: HFI ({{c1::aldolase B}} deficiency): F1P traps {{c2::phosphate}}, causing hypoglycemia after fructose; {{c3::fructokinase}} deficiency is benign.

why: Insulin vs glucagon control of blood glucose is the central fed/fasting concept

front: How does Cori disease (debrancher deficiency) differ biochemically from Von Gierke disease?
why: Cori vs Von Gierke comparison is glycogen-storage-disease minutiae

front: In untreated type 1 diabetes, blood glucose is high yet tissues behave as if {{c1::starving}}, because {{c2::insulin}} is absent.

front: Insulin binds a {{c1::receptor tyrosine kinase}} that autophosphorylates and signals through IRS and {{c2::PI3K-Akt}} to move GLUT4 to the surface.

front: Intestinal glucose uptake uses {{c1::SGLT1}}, a $Na^+$-coupled {{c2::secondary active}} transporter, while fructose enters passively through {{c3::GLUT5}}.

front: Iodoacetate blocks glycolysis by alkylating the active-site {{c1::cysteine}} of {{c2::glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase}}.

front: Lactase deficiency is confirmed by a {{c1::hydrogen breath}} test because colonic bacteria ferment the undigested {{c2::lactose}}.

front: Metformin lowers glucose by suppressing hepatic {{c1::gluconeogenesis}} and activating {{c2::AMPK}}; its rare serious toxicity is {{c3::lactic acidosis}}.
why: Metformin mechanism is drug detail; passage would supply it

front: Normal fasting plasma glucose is {{c1::70-100}} mg/dL, and diabetes is diagnosed at a fasting value of {{c2::126}} mg/dL or above.
why: Diagnostic glucose thresholds are numeric clinical trivia not on the outline

front: Phosphorylase kinase is fully active when phosphorylated by {{c1::PKA}} AND bound by {{c2::$Ca^{2+}$-calmodulin}} (its delta subunit).

front: Pyruvate carboxylase is located in the {{c1::mitochondrial matrix}}, uses the cofactor {{c2::biotin}}, and requires the allosteric activator {{c3::acetyl-CoA}}.

front: Pyruvate kinase: feedforward-activated by {{c1::F1,6BP}}, inhibited by ATP and {{c2::alanine}}; liver isozyme inactivated by {{c3::PKA phosphorylation}}.

why: RBCs lacking mitochondria and relying on glycolysis is a classic
